entries.test: Public results from increasing LLM data and parameter counts would show whether pure scaling reaches a performance ceiling and fails to eliminate hallucinations and basic errors; scaling-law research would establish the laws' empirical status.
entries.note: This combines an undated prediction with an observation about scaling laws.
Bluffing asserts conscious misrepresentation; disappointing results alone cannot establish Altman's private knowledge or intention.

entries.test: OpenAI's public announcements and documented naming history would establish whether Orion was designated GPT-4.5 after previously being intended as GPT-5.
entries.note: Calling the naming a downgrade requires evidence of the prior intended designation.

entries.test: Public reporting on Orion's development, scaling experiments, and achieved capabilities would establish whether it failed its intended GPT-5 goals and whether additional pure scaling had stopped producing improvements.
entries.note: The surrounding discussion supplies a plain reading of failure: falling short of the intended GPT-5 advance.
Both the disappointed reactions and reputational damage are explicitly probabilistic.
Neither 'truly revolutionary' nor the company's 'future' supplies a shared criterion for the asserted dependency.

entries.test: Public GPT-5 technical documentation and release disclosures would establish whether OpenAI used approaches beyond increasing training data and parameter counts.
entries.note: GPT-5's release occurred before the evaluation date, making the forecast assessable.
The normalization removes 'appears' from the domain comparison. Test-time compute is a firm, separately checkable forecast, but massive synthetic-data use is explicitly a suspicion.
The scaling-law shortfall is explicitly qualified by 'likely'; the assertion about Altman's knowledge is implied by the argument.

entries.test: Public evidence of continued AI research, development, and deployment after the claimed exhaustion of pure scaling would establish whether AI continued.
entries.note: 'AI will go on' commits to continuation; 'continue to progress' adds a stronger claim of improvement.
Both AGI's arrival and the inclusion of other components are qualified by likelihood.

entries.test: Public comparisons of scaling-law predictions with measured model performance, together with investment totals and documented investment rationales, would test the asserted failure of data-and-parameter-only prediction and its half-trillion-dollar industry role.
entries.note: In context, 'dead' asserts that the predictive thesis has failed, rather than that literally nobody believes it.

entries.test: A publicly documented and independently validated method for achieving AGI that existed by the publication date would refute the claim.
entries.note: The plain reading concerns an established technical solution; undisclosed possibilities do not make that claim uncheckable.

entries.test: Public scaling experiments and capability evaluations would test scaling's benefits and whether increasing data and parameters alone provides a sufficient route to AGI.
entries.note: The surrounding discussion identifies AGI as the problem for which scaling is claimed to be insufficient.
